name: ChatGPT to Word
tagline: Paste a ChatGPT conversation or its markdown and get back a formatted .docx file.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a format converter wearing a domain name. Markdown to .docx is a solved problem with mature open libraries, and the whole thing can run in the browser tab with no server, no account, and no upload. The only genuinely fiddly parts are the bits people forget about: code blocks that keep their monospace and indentation, nested lists, tables, and LaTeX math that ChatGPT emits as dollar signs. An agent can get you a working converter in a session and you will spend the rest of your time tuning styles until headings stop looking like a ransom note. Paying for this makes sense only if you convert one document a year and would rather not think about it.
coreLoopDIY: A single static page where you paste markdown or a copied chat thread, pick a style preset, and download a .docx with real Word heading styles, lists, tables, and monospaced code blocks.
requirements: Node and npm to build the static bundle
A browser; everything runs client side
Optional: Word or LibreOffice to check that the styles actually render
whatYouLose: Someone else's taste in default typography and spacing, which is most of the perceived quality here
Edge case handling for weird paste artifacts: copied UI chrome, role labels, collapsed thinking blocks
Math rendering, unless you wire up a LaTeX to OMML step yourself
Other output targets like PDF or Google Docs if the paid tool offers them
A hosted URL you can use from a phone or a machine you do not control
moatNotes: The moat is a nice-looking default template and the fact that nobody wants to debug docx XML on a Tuesday.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the pain is acute and rare. You need the transcript in Word right now for a client, a professor, or a compliance folder, and a link that works in ten seconds beats a build, even a fast one. The paid version also absorbs the long tail of malformed input, which is exactly the part your own converter will choke on the first time you paste something odd.
notes: A converter with a landing page is still a converter, and this one is honest about it.
prompt:
Build a single-page, fully client-side markdown to .docx converter. No backend, no accounts, no analytics, no network calls at runtime.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Vite + TypeScript, vanilla DOM, no framework
- 'marked' to parse markdown into tokens
- 'docx' (npm) to build the document
- 'file-saver' to trigger the download
- Plain CSS, no UI library

UI: one page, two columns. Left is a large textarea for pasted markdown or a copied chat thread. Right is a small panel with a style preset selector (Report, Manuscript, Compact), a checkbox for 'include a title page', a checkbox for 'strip role labels like You: and ChatGPT:', and a big Download .docx button. Show a live token count and a warning if the input is empty.

Conversion rules that must work:
- Headings h1 to h4 map to real Word heading styles so Word's navigation pane and TOC work
- Ordered and unordered lists, including two levels of nesting
- Fenced code blocks: monospaced font, preserved line breaks and leading whitespace, light grey shading, no smart quotes
- Inline code: monospaced with subtle shading
- Tables from GFM pipe syntax, with a bold header row and thin borders
- Bold, italic, strikethrough, blockquotes, horizontal rules
- Links become Word hyperlinks with the visible text preserved
- Images referenced by URL are skipped, with a bracketed placeholder noting the skip

Input cleanup: when the strip option is on, detect lines that are only a speaker label and convert them into a styled 'speaker' paragraph instead of body text.

Out of scope, do not build: LaTeX math conversion, PDF export, file uploads, .docx import, cloud storage, sharing links, any server.

Deliverables: working app on 'npm run dev', a static build via 'npm run build', a README with the three style presets described, and three sample markdown fixtures in /samples covering code blocks, nested lists, and tables. If you ever add an API key for anything, put it in .env and .gitignore it, but this build should need none.
